claim: A quarter of the human population is infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
source: A quarter of the human population is infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, but less than 10% of those infected develop pulmonary TB.
evidence: This is a statement of epidemiological fact supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2022 in the Introduction.

claim: Less than 10% of those infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis develop pulmonary TB.
source: A quarter of the human population is infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, but less than 10% of those infected develop pulmonary TB.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the Introduction (Behr et al., 2021; Drain et al., 2018; Horsburgh and Rubin, 2011; Reichler et al., 2018).

claim: The sst1-susceptible mouse model uniquely reproduces the development of necrotic lung granulomas, a defining feature of human TB.
source: We developed a genetically defined sst1-susceptible mouse model that uniquely reproduces a defining feature of human TB: the development of necrotic lung granulomas
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study and prior publications (Kramnik et al., 1998; Kramnik et al., 2000; Sissons et al., 2009).

claim: The sst1-susceptible phenotype is driven by aberrant macrophage activation.
source: We developed a genetically defined sst1-susceptible mouse model that uniquely reproduces a defining feature of human TB: the development of necrotic lung granulomas and determined that the sst1-susceptible phenotype was driven by the aberrant macrophage activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including in vitro macrophage studies and in vivo lesion analysis.

claim: The aberrant response of sst1-susceptible macrophages to prolonged TNF stimulation is primarily driven by conflicting Myc and antioxidant response pathways.
source: This study demonstrates that the aberrant response of the sst1-susceptible macrophages to prolonged stimulation with TNF is primarily driven by conflicting Myc and antioxidant response pathways leading to a coordinated failure (1) to properly sequester intracellular iron and (2) to activate ferroptosis inhibitor enzymes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including RNA-seq, protein analysis, and functional assays presented in Figures 2-5.

claim: Sst1-susceptible macrophages fail to properly sequester intracellular iron.
source: This study demonstrates that the aberrant response of the sst1-susceptible macrophages to prolonged stimulation with TNF is primarily driven by conflicting Myc and antioxidant response pathways leading to a coordinated failure (1) to properly sequester intracellular iron and (2) to activate ferroptosis inhibitor enzymes.
evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced ferritin expression and increased labile iron pool in B6.Sst1S macrophages (Figure 3).

claim: Sst1-susceptible macrophages fail to activate ferroptosis inhibitor enzymes.
source: This study demonstrates that the aberrant response of the sst1-susceptible macrophages to prolonged stimulation with TNF is primarily driven by conflicting Myc and antioxidant response pathways leading to a coordinated failure (1) to properly sequester intracellular iron and (2) to activate ferroptosis inhibitor enzymes.
evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced Gpx4 expression in B6.Sst1S macrophages (Figure 3D).

claim: Iron-mediated lipid peroxidation fuels superinduction of Ifnβ in sst1-susceptible macrophages.
source: Consequently, iron-mediated lipid peroxidation fueled superinduction of Ifnβ and sustained the type I interferon (IFN-I) pathway hyperactivity that locked the sst1-susceptible macrophages in a state of unresolving stress and compromised their resistance to Mtb.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that lipid peroxidation inhibitors prevent Ifnβ superinduction (Figure 4F-G).

claim: Type I interferon pathway hyperactivity locks sst1-susceptible macrophages in a state of unresolving stress.
source: Consequently, iron-mediated lipid peroxidation fueled superinduction of Ifnβ and sustained the type I interferon (IFN-I) pathway hyperactivity that locked the sst1-susceptible macrophages in a state of unresolving stress and compromised their resistance to Mtb.
evidence: This is supported by data showing persistent stress markers and that IFNAR1 blockade reduces stress and improves Mtb control (Figures 3K, 6L-M).

claim: The aberrant macrophage activation compromises resistance to Mtb.
source: Consequently, iron-mediated lipid peroxidation fueled superinduction of Ifnβ and sustained the type I interferon (IFN-I) pathway hyperactivity that locked the sst1-susceptible macrophages in a state of unresolving stress and compromised their resistance to Mtb.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro infection data showing reduced Mtb control by B6.Sst1S macrophages (Figure 6C, F, H).

claim: The accumulation of aberrantly activated, stressed macrophages within the granuloma microenvironment leads to local failure of anti-tuberculosis immunity and tissue necrosis.
source: The accumulation of the aberrantly activated, stressed, macrophages within the granuloma microenvironment led to the local failure of anti-tuberculosis immunity and tissue necrosis.
evidence: This is supported by spatial transcriptomics and immunohistochemistry data from TB lesions (Figure 7).

claim: Upregulation of the Myc pathway in peripheral blood cells of human TB patients is significantly associated with poor outcomes of TB treatment.
source: The upregulation of the Myc pathway in peripheral blood cells of human TB patients was significantly associated with poor outcomes of TB treatment.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of blood transcriptomes from TB patients showing Myc_up signature enrichment in treatment failures (Figure 8).

claim: Myc dysregulation in activated macrophages results in aberrant macrophage activation.
source: Thus, Myc dysregulation in activated macrophages results in an aberrant macrophage activation and represents a novel target for host-directed TB therapies.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that Myc inhibition prevents aberrant activation markers and improves Mtb control (Figure 5).

claim: Myc dysregulation represents a novel target for host-directed TB therapies.
source: Thus, Myc dysregulation in activated macrophages results in an aberrant macrophage activation and represents a novel target for host-directed TB therapies.
evidence: This is based on inference from experimental data showing therapeutic effects of Myc inhibition and association with human TB outcomes.

claim: Mtb currently colonizes approximately a quarter of the global population.
source: It currently colonizes approximately a quarter of the global population (World Health Organization, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2022.

claim: About 5-10% of Mtb-infected individuals will eventually develop active TB.
source: However, about 5–10% of Mtb-infected individuals will eventually develop active TB either within a year after the primary infection or later in their life after re-activation of persistent bacteria or re-infection (Behr et al., 2021; Drain et al., 2018; Horsburgh and Rubin, 2011; Reichler et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Behr et al., 2021; Drain et al., 2018; Horsburgh and Rubin, 2011; Reichler et al., 2018).

claim: Approximately 85% of TB disease develops in the lungs.
source: However, approximately 85% of the disease develops in the lungs (Pai et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pai et al., 2016.

claim: Necrotic lesions are the major pathologic manifestation of pulmonary TB.
source: Necrotic lesions are the major pathologic manifestation of pulmonary TB ranging from central necrosis in organized granulomas during primary TB to massive necrotizing pneumonia and the formation of cavities in post-primary pulmonary TB (Hunter, 2011; Pai et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Hunter, 2011; Pai et al., 2016).

claim: Classical inbred mouse strains C57BL/6 and BALB/c do not develop human-like necrotic TB lesions.
source: Mouse models have been successfully used for mechanistic studies of Mtb infection, although classical inbred mouse strains routinely used in TB research, such as C57BL/6 (B6) and BALB/c, do not develop human-like necrotic TB lesions (Apt and Kramnik, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Apt and Kramnik, 2009.

claim: C3HeB/FeJ mice develop necrotizing granulomas after infection with virulent Mtb.
source: We have previously found that C3HeB/FeJ mice develop necrotizing granulomas after infection with virulent Mtb and mapped several genetic loci of TB susceptibility using a cross of the C3HeB/FeJ with the resistant B6 mice (Kramnik et al., 1998; Kramnik et al., 2000; Yan et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Kramnik et al., 1998; Kramnik et al., 2000; Yan et al., 2006).

claim: The sst1 locus is specifically responsible for the control of necrotization of TB lesions.
source: A single locus on chromosome 1, sst1 (supersusceptibility to tuberculosis 1), was specifically responsible for the control of the necrotization of TB lesions (Sissons et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sissons et al., 2009.

claim: Sst1-susceptible mice develop necrotic lung lesions irrespective of the route of infection.
source: The sst1-susceptible mice develop necrotic lung lesions irrespective of the route of infection – aerosol, intravenous, or intradermal (Kramnik et al., 1998; Kramnik et al., 2000; Pan et al., 2005; Pichugin et al., 2009; Yabaji et al., 2025b) – thus demonstrating a common underlying mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Kramnik et al., 1998; Kramnik et al., 2000; Pan et al., 2005; Pichugin et al., 2009; Yabaji et al., 2025b).

claim: The sst1 locus primarily controls innate resistance to intracellular pathogens.
source: We further found that the sst1 locus primarily controls innate resistance to intracellular pathogens (Boyartchuk et al., 2004; He et al., 2013; Pan et al., 2005; Yan et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations (Boyartchuk et al., 2004; He et al., 2013; Pan et al., 2005; Yan et al., 2007).

claim: Sst1-mediated susceptibility is associated with hyperactivity of the type I interferon pathway in activated macrophages.
source: and the sst1-mediated susceptibility was associated with the hyperactivity of the type I interferon (IFN-I) pathway in activated macrophages in vitro and in vivo (Bhattacharya et al., 2021; He et al., 2013; Ji et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Bhattacharya et al., 2021; He et al., 2013; Ji et al., 2019).

claim: Hyperactivity of the IFN-I pathway has been associated with TB susceptibility and disease progression in human patients and experimental models.
source: Of note, the hyperactivity of the IFN-I pathway has been associated with TB susceptibility and the disease progression both in human patients and experimental models (Donovan et al., 2017; Moreira-Teixeira et al., 2018; O'Garra et al., 2013; Stanley et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Donovan et al., 2017; Moreira-Teixeira et al., 2018; O'Garra et al., 2013; Stanley et al., 2007).

claim: The sst1 locus encodes the Sp110 and Sp140 proteins.
source: The sst1 locus encodes the Sp110 (Pan et al., 2005) and Sp140 (Ji et al., 2021) proteins – known as interferon-inducible chromatin binding proteins (Fraschilla and Jeffrey, 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Pan et al., 2005; Ji et al., 2021; Fraschilla and Jeffrey, 2020a).

claim: Expression of Sp110 and Sp140 mRNAs is greatly diminished in mice carrying the sst1 susceptibility allele.
source: The expression of mRNAs encoding both proteins is greatly diminished in mice that carry the sst1 susceptibility allele, and protein expression is undetectable for both (Bhattacharya et al., 2021; Ji et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Bhattacharya et al., 2021; Ji et al., 2021).

claim: Sp110 and Sp140 proteins are involved in regulation of type I interferon pathway.
source: Both proteins were shown to be involved in regulation of type I interferon pathway (Ji et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Ji et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2013).

claim: Overexpression of Sp110b in macrophages increased their resistance to intracellular bacteria in vitro.
source: The overexpression of Sp110b in macrophages increased their resistance to intracellular bacteria in vitro (Pan et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pan et al., 2005.

claim: Sp140 gene knockout dramatically increased mouse susceptibility to several intracellular bacteria including virulent Mtb.
source: while the Sp140 gene knockout dramatically increased the mouse susceptibility to several intracellular bacteria including virulent Mtb (Ji et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ji et al., 2021.

claim: Sp140 plays a dominant role in TB susceptibility via direct regulation of Ifnb1 mRNA stability.
source: It was suggested that Sp140 plays a dominant role in TB susceptibility, via direct regulation of the interferon beta gene (Ifnb1) mRNA stability (Witt et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Witt et al., 2024.

claim: Sp140 hypomorphic alleles are associated with susceptibility to multiple sclerosis and Crohn's disease in humans.
source: In humans, the Sp140 hypomorphic alleles were associated with susceptibility to multiple sclerosis and Crohn's disease (Matesanz et al., 2015; Mehta et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Matesanz et al., 2015; Mehta et al., 2017).

claim: Sp140 mutations predict responsiveness of Crohn's disease patients to anti-TNF therapy.
source: Moreover, the Sp140 mutations predicted the responsiveness of Crohn's disease patients to anti-TNF therapy, suggesting its role in regulating TNF response.
evidence: This is based on inference from the cited literature on Sp140 in Crohn's disease.

claim: Sp140 is implicated in silencing 'lineage-inappropriate' and developmental genes and maintenance of heterochromatin in activated macrophages.
source: Mechanistically, Sp140 was implicated in silencing 'lineage-inappropriate' and developmental genes, maintenance of heterochromatin in activated macrophages (Mehta et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mehta et al., 2017.

claim: Sp140 downregulates transcriptional activity by inhibiting topoisomerases.
source: and downregulating transcriptional activity by inhibiting topoisomerases (Amatullah et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Amatullah et al., 2022.

claim: Prolonged TNF stimulation of B6.Sst1S macrophages induces Ifnb1 superinduction and coordinated upregulation of interferon-stimulated genes, proteotoxic stress markers, and integrated stress response markers.
source: Previously, we found that prolonged TNF stimulation of the sst1-susceptible B6.Sst1S macrophages in vitro uniquely induced an aberrant response that was characterized by the Ifnb1 superinduction and a coordinated upregulation of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs), markers of proteotoxic stress (PS), and the integrated stress response (ISR).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Bhattacharya et al., 2021).

claim: Upregulation of stress pathways in B6.Sst1S macrophages was prevented by a reactive oxygen scavenger (BHA).
source: The upregulation of all these pathways was prevented by a reactive oxygen scavenger (BHA; Bhattacharya et al., 2021), suggesting that oxidative stress was driving the aberrant activation of the sst1-susceptible macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bhattacharya et al., 2021.

claim: Oxidative stress drives the aberrant activation of sst1-susceptible macrophages.
source: The upregulation of all these pathways was prevented by a reactive oxygen scavenger (BHA; Bhattacharya et al., 2021), suggesting that oxidative stress was driving the aberrant activation of the sst1-susceptible macrophages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effect of ROS scavenger.

claim: Stress kinases are activated by oxidative stress.
source: (1) stress kinase activation by oxidative stress (Blaser et al., 2016; Kamata et al., 2005);
evidence: This is supported by citations (Blaser et al., 2016; Kamata et al., 2005).

claim: Stress kinases promote type I interferon responses.
source: (2) promotion of type I interferon (IFN-I) responses by stress kinases (Boccuni et al., 2022; Buskiewicz et al., 2016; Karin and Gallagher, 2005);
evidence: This is supported by citations (Boccuni et al., 2022; Buskiewicz et al., 2016; Karin and Gallagher, 2005).

claim: IFN-I suppresses antioxidant defense.
source: (3) suppression of AOD by IFN-I (Lei et al., 2021; Riedelberger et al., 2020);
evidence: This is supported by citations (Lei et al., 2021; Riedelberger et al., 2020).

claim: Myc suppresses IFN responses and antioxidant defense.
source: (4) suppression of IFN responses and AOD by Myc (Levy and Forman, 2010; Torti and Torti, 2002; Zimmerli et al., 2022; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Levy and Forman, 2010; Torti and Torti, 2002; Zimmerli et al., 2022).

claim: Naive macrophage populations of B6 and B6.Sst1S backgrounds are similar.
source: The naive macrophage populations of both backgrounds were similar.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data presented in Figure 1B-C.

claim: All BMDMs responded to TNF stimulation, as evidenced by de novo formation of clusters 1-6.
source: All BMDMs responded to TNF stimulation, as evidenced by the de novo formation of clusters 1–6, where cluster 3 appeared exclusively in the resistant (B6) and clusters 4 and 5 in the susceptible (B6.Sst1S) macrophage populations (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cluster 3 appeared exclusively in resistant B6 macrophages after TNF stimulation.
source: All BMDMs responded to TNF stimulation, as evidenced by the de novo formation of clusters 1–6, where cluster 3 appeared exclusively in the resistant (B6) and clusters 4 and 5 in the susceptible (B6.Sst1S) macrophage populations (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Clusters 4 and 5 appeared exclusively in susceptible B6.Sst1S macrophages after TNF stimulation.
source: All BMDMs responded to TNF stimulation, as evidenced by the de novo formation of clusters 1–6, where cluster 3 appeared exclusively in the resistant (B6) and clusters 4 and 5 in the susceptible (B6.Sst1S) macrophage populations (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Expression of Sp110 and Sp140 genes coordinately increased only in B6 macrophages after TNF stimulation.
source: After TNF stimulation, the expression of the sst1-encoded Sp110 and Sp140 genes coordinately increased only in the B6 macrophages (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The IFN pathway was dramatically upregulated in TNF-stimulated B6.Sst1S cells that lacked Sp110 and Sp140 expression.
source: The IFN pathway was dramatically upregulated in TNF-stimulated B6.Sst1S cells that lacked the Sp110 and Sp140 expression, but it was upregulated to a lesser degree in cluster 3 exclusive for TNF-stimulated Sp110/140-positive B6 macrophages (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq pathway analysis shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TNF stimulation increased the fraction of macrophages in S phase.
source: Cell cycle analysis demonstrated that TNF stimulation increased the fraction of macrophages in S phase (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle analysis data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The transition from sp2 to sp3 in resistant B6 BMDMs was characterized by an increase of the G1/S ratio.
source: The transition from sp2 to sp3 in the resistant B6 BMDMs was characterized by an increase of the G1/S ratio, the downregulation of anabolic pathways involved in cell growth and replication (E2F and Myc), and the upregulation of anti-oxidant genes (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: The transition from sp2 to sp3 in resistant B6 BMDMs was characterized by downregulation of E2F and Myc pathways.
source: The transition from sp2 to sp3 in the resistant B6 BMDMs was characterized by an increase of the G1/S ratio, the downregulation of anabolic pathways involved in cell growth and replication (E2F and Myc), and the upregulation of anti-oxidant genes (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: The transition from sp2 to sp3 in resistant B6 BMDMs was characterized by upregulation of anti-oxidant genes.
source: The transition from sp2 to sp3 in the resistant B6 BMDMs was characterized by an increase of the G1/S ratio, the downregulation of anabolic pathways involved in cell growth and replication (E2F and Myc), and the upregulation of anti-oxidant genes (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: In susceptible B6.Sst1S macrophages, sp2 transitioned to sp4 and sp5 with decreased G1/S ratios compared to sp3.
source: In contrast, in the susceptible B6.Sst1S macrophages, the sp2 transitioned to subpopulations sp4 and sp5 that were characterized by the decreased G1/S ratios as compared to sp3, signifying an increased G1 – S transition (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis and cell cycle data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Subpopulation sp4 was primarily characterized by upregulation of the IFN pathway.
source: The sp4 represented an intermediate state between sp2 and sp5 and was primarily characterized by the upregulation of the IFN pathway (Figure 1G), as evidenced by the upregulation of known IFN-I pathway activation markers Rsad2, IL1rn, Cxcl10; (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Subpopulation sp5 uniquely demonstrated coordinated upregulation of IFN, TGFβ, Myc, E2F, and stress response pathways.
source: The ST macrophages in sp5 uniquely demonstrated a coordinated upregulation of the IFN, TGFβ, Myc, E2F, and stress response (p53 and UPR) pathways (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Subpopulation sp5 upregulated ISR genes in parallel with markers of immune suppression and apoptosis.
source: They upregulated the ISR genes (Ddit3/Chop10, Atf3, Ddit4, Trib1, Trib3, Chac1) in parallel with markers of immune suppression and apoptosis (Cd274/PD-L1, Fas, Trail/Tnfsf10, Id2, and a pro-apoptotic ligand – receptor pair Tnfsf12/Tweak and Tnfrsf12a/Tweak receptor; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: IFN-I pathway genes were upregulated in all TNF-stimulated B6.Sst1S macrophages in agreement with the paracrine effect of Ifnβ.
source: Of note, IFN-I pathway genes were upregulated in all TNF-stimulated B6.Sst1S macrophages in agreement with the paracrine effect of Ifnβ, whose increased production by TNF-stimulated B6.Sst1S macrophages we have described previously (Bhattacharya et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data and citation to Bhattacharya et al., 2021.

claim: Expression of Irf7 and several IFN-inducible genes was reduced in sp5 cells, suggesting partial dampening of IFN-I responsiveness.
source: Interestingly, the expression of Irf7 and several IFN-inducible genes, such as B2m, Cxcl10, and Ube2l6 was reduced in the sp5 cells, suggesting partial dampening of their IFN-I responsiveness (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an inference based on gene expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Subpopulation sp5 represents a terminal state of aberrant B6.Sst1S macrophage activation by TNF.
source: Taken together, the single-cell trajectory analysis revealed that sp5 represented a terminal state of the aberrant B6.Sst1S macrophage activation by TNF that was characterized by the coordinated upregulation of stress, pro-apoptotic, and immunosuppression genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on trajectory analysis data.

claim: In resistant macrophages, the sst1 locus-encoded genes promoted activation of the AOD pathway either directly or by suppressing the IFN-I pathway.
source: Therefore, we concluded that in resistant TNF-stimulated macrophages, the sst1 locus-encoded genes promoted the activation of the AOD pathway either directly or by suppressing the IFN-I pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on inference from trajectory analysis data.

claim: Sp110 and Sp140 genes co-expressed with targets of Nfe2l1/2 and Mtf transcription factors in mouse macrophages.
source: This analysis revealed that in mouse macrophages, the Sp110 and Sp140 genes co-expressed with targets of Nfe2l1/2 (Nuclear Factor Erythroid 2 Like 1/2) and Mtf (metal-responsive transcription factor) TFs that are involved in regulating macrophage responses to oxidative stress and heavy metals, respectively (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by gene regulatory network analysis shown in Figure 1I.

claim: In TNF-stimulated macrophages, Sp110 and/or Sp140 might be primarily involved in regulating antioxidant defense.
source: Taken together, our experimental data and the unbiased network analysis suggested that in TNF-stimulated macrophages, the sst1-encoded Sp110 and/or Sp140 gene(s) might be primarily involved in regulating AOD.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and network analysis.

claim: Nrf2 protein levels were higher in TNF-stimulated B6 BMDMs compared to B6.Sst1S BMDMs at 8-12 hours.
source: Comparing the time course of major transcriptional regulators of AOD in TNF-stimulated B6 and B6.Sst1S macrophages during this critical time interval, we observed higher upregulation of Nrf2 protein in TNF-stimulated B6 BMDMs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Nrf1 levels were not substantially upregulated after TNF stimulation and were similar in B6 and B6.Sst1S BMDMs.
source: The Nrf1 levels were not substantially upregulated after TNF stimulation and were similar in B6 and B6.Sst1S BMDMs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot and microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Nrf2 difference was observed both in cytoplasmic and nuclear fractions.
source: The Nrf2 difference was observed both in cytoplasmic and nuclear fractions (Figure 2B and C, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Levels of Nrf2 negative regulators Keap1, β-TrCP, and Bach1 were similar in both backgrounds and did not notably change after TNF stimulation.
source: The levels of Nrf2 negative regulators Keap1 and β-TrCP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), and Bach1 (Figure 2B and C) were similar in both backgrounds and did not notably change after TNF stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B, C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cytoplasmic and nuclear Nrf2 levels significantly increased in B6 but not in B6.Sst1S BMDMs at 12 hr of TNF stimulation.
source: Quantitative microscopy confirmed that at 12 hr of TNF stimulation, the cytoplasmic and nuclear Nrf2 levels significantly increased in B6 but not in B6.Sst1S BMDMs (Figure 2D and E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 2D, E, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Levels of Nfe2l1/2 mRNA induced by TNF were higher in B6.Sst1S macrophages, suggesting post-transcriptional regulation.
source: In contrast, the levels of Nfe2l1/2 mRNA induced by TNF were higher in the mutant macrophages, suggesting post-transcriptional regulation (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is an inference based on qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: No difference in rates of Nrf2 protein degradation was found between B6 and B6.Sst1S macrophages 6-8 hr after TNF stimulation.
source: Therefore, we measured the rates of Nrf2 protein degradation 6–8 hr after TNF stimulation but found no difference (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: This is supported by cycloheximide chase assay data shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: Binding activity of nuclear Nrf2 to its target DNA at 8 and 12 hr after TNF stimulation was greater in resistant B6 BMDMs.
source: Using EMSA, we demonstrated that binding activity of nuclear Nrf2 to its target DNA at 8 and 12 hr after TNF stimulation was greater in the resistant B6 BMDMs (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: IFN response, Myc, E2F target gene, Hypoxia, UV response, and DNA repair pathways were upregulated in TNF-stimulated B6.Sst1S macrophages at 12 hr.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of genes differentially expressed between TNF-stimulated B6.Sst1S and B6 macrophages at this critical junction revealed that the IFN response, Myc, E2F target gene, Hypoxia, UV response, and DNA repair pathways were upregulated in the mutant macrophages, while the detoxification of reactive oxygen species, cholesterol homeostasis, fatty acid metabolism, and oxidative phosphorylation, peroxisome, and lysosome pathways were downregulated (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Detoxification of reactive oxygen species, cholesterol homeostasis, fatty acid metabolism, oxidative phosphorylation, peroxisome, and lysosome pathways were downregulated in TNF-stimulated B6.Sst1S macrophages at 12 hr.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of genes differentially expressed between TNF-stimulated B6.Sst1S and B6 macrophages at this critical junction revealed that the IFN response, Myc, E2F target gene, Hypoxia, UV response, and DNA repair pathways were upregulated in the mutant macrophages, while the detoxification of reactive oxygen species, cholesterol homeostasis, fatty acid metabolism, and oxidative phosphorylation, peroxisome, and lysosome pathways were downregulated (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Wild-type macrophages upregulated genes involved in detoxification of reactive oxygen species, inhibition of ferroptosis, and peroxisome function.
source: In contrast, the wild-type macrophages upregulated genes involved in detoxification of reactive oxygen species, inhibition of ferroptosis, and peroxisome function (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis in Supplementary file 4.

claim: Total antioxidant capacity of B6 macrophages after TNF stimulation increased to significantly higher levels compared to B6.Sst1S.
source: Supporting these findings, the total antioxidant capacity of the B6 macrophages after TNF stimulation increased to significantly higher levels, as compared to the B6.Sst1S (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by antioxidant capacity assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Genes specifically upregulated by TNF in B6 but not B6.Sst1S macrophages showed enrichment of Nfe2l1/Nfe2l2, Bach1, and Mafk sequence motifs.
source: Transcription factor binding site analysis of genes specifically upregulated by TNF in B6, but not B6.Sst1S, macrophages (B6-specific cluster) revealed an enrichment of Nfe2l1/Nfe2l2, Bach1, and Mafk sequence motifs, that is binding sites of transcription factors regulating AOD.
evidence: This is supported by transcription factor binding site analysis in Supplementary file 5.

claim: Genes in the Sst1S-specific cluster showed overrepresentation of E2F, Egr1, and Pbx3 transcription factor binding sites.
source: In contrast, overrepresentation of E2F, Egr1, and Pbx3 transcription factor binding sites was found for genes in the Sst1S-specific cluster (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by transcription factor binding site analysis in Supplementary file 5.

claim: Master regulator analysis revealed a key role for Nfe2l1/2 transcription factors as regulators of genes differentially induced by TNF in B6 and B6.Sst1S BMDMs.
source: A master regulator analysis using Virtual Inference of Protein Activity by Enriched Regulon Analysis (VIPER) algorithm also revealed a key role for Nfe2l1/2 (NF-E2-like) transcription factors (TFs) as regulators of genes differentially induced by TNF in B6 and B6.Sst1S BMDMs (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is supported by VIPER analysis in Supplementary file 6.

claim: Response to oxidative stress in sst1 mutant macrophages was dysregulated but not paralyzed.
source: This analysis demonstrated that the response to oxidative stress in the sst1 mutant macrophages was dysregulated, but not paralyzed.
evidence: This is an inference based on gene expression analysis of oxidative stress genes.

claim: Upregulation of Hmox1 and Nqo1 was similar in B6 and B6.Sst1S BMDMs.
source: For example, the upregulation of well-known Nrf2 target genes Heme oxygenase 1 (Hmox1) and (NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1) (Nqo1) was similar in B6 and B6.Sst1S BMDMs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: A subset of antioxidant defense genes whose expression was concordant with Sp110 and Sp140 in B6 macrophages includes genes involved in iron storage, ROS detoxification, and maintenance of redox state.
source: A subset of antioxidant defense genes whose expression was concordant with Sp110 and Sp140 in B6 macrophages represented genes that are known to be involved in iron storage (ferritin light and heavy chains, Ftl and Fth), ROS detoxification and maintenance of redox state (Cat, G6pdx, Sod2, Gstm1, Gpx4, Prdx6, Srxn1, Txn2, and Txnrd1; Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Coordinate downregulation of AOD genes in TNF-stimulated B6.Sst1S macrophages sensitized the mutant cells to iron-mediated oxidative damage.
source: We hypothesized that their coordinate downregulation in TNF-stimulated B6.Sst1S macrophages sensitized the mutant cells to iron-mediated oxidative damage and played a pivotal role in shaping their divergent activation trajectory.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on gene expression data.

claim: Fth mRNA was upregulated by TNF in B6 BMDMs but remained at basal level in B6.Sst1S cells.
source: While the Fth mRNA was upregulated by TNF in B6 BMDMs, it remained at a basal level in the B6.Sst1S cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Ftl mRNA level was significantly reduced after TNF stimulation in B6.Sst1S macrophages but remained at basal level in B6.
source: The Ftl mRNA level was significantly reduced after TNF stimulation in B6.Sst1S macrophages but remained at the basal level in B6 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Expression of Ftl protein was reduced in B6.Sst1S BMDMs after 12 hr of TNF stimulation, and both Ftl and Fth proteins were reduced at 24 hr.
source: Accordingly, the expression of Ftl protein was reduced in B6.Sst1S BMDMs after 12 hr of TNF stimulation, and both Ftl and Fth proteins were reduced at 24 hr (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Levels of Gpx1 and Gpx4 proteins were substantially reduced by 24 hr in B6.Sst1S macrophages.
source: In parallel, the levels of Gpx1 and Gpx4 proteins were also substantially reduced by 24 hr in B6.Sst1S (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Gpx4 plays a central role in preventing ferroptosis because of its unique ability to reduce hydroperoxide in complex membrane phospholipids.
source: The glutathione peroxidase 4 (Gpx4) protein plays a central role in preventing ferroptosis because of its unique ability to reduce hydroperoxide in complex membrane phospholipids and, thus, limit self-catalytic lipid peroxidation (Stockwell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stockwell et al., 2017.

claim: TNF-stimulated B6.Sst1S BMDMs had reduced intracellular iron storage capacity accompanied by decline of Gpx4.
source: Thus, TNF-stimulated B6.Sst1S BMDMs had reduced intracellular iron storage capacity accompanied by the decline of the major lipid peroxidation inhibitor Gpx4.
evidence: This is an inference based on ferritin and Gpx4 protein data.

claim: Increases in labile iron pool, oxidized lipids, MDA, and 4-HNE adducts were observed in TNF-stimulated B6.Sst1S macrophages.
source: Accordingly, we observed increases in an intracellular labile iron pool (LIP, Figure 3E), an intracellular accumulation of oxidized lipids (Figure 3F), a toxic terminal lipid peroxidation (LPO) products malondialdehyde (MDA, Figure 3G) and 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE) adducts (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by multiple assay data shown in Figure 3E-H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment with lipid peroxidation inhibitor Ferrostatin-1 prevented 4-HNE adducts accumulation.
source: Treatment with the LPO inhibitor Ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1) prevented the 4-HNE adducts accumulation (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Levels of LIP and LPO remained significantly elevated in B6.Sst1S macrophages after 48 hr of TNF stimulation.
source: The levels of the LIP and LPO remained significantly elevated in B6.Sst1S macrophages after 48 hr of TNF stimulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-F).
evidence: This is supported by assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-F.

claim: Increased ROS production was observed in B6.Sst1S macrophages during persistent TNF stimulation.
source: We also observed an increased ROS production in the B6.Sst1S macrophages during persistent TNF stimulation (Figure 3I and J, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by ROS assay data shown in Figure 3I, J, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: ASK1-JNK-cJun stress kinase axis was upregulated in B6.Sst1S macrophages 12-36 hr after TNF stimulation.
source: The ASK1 - JNK – cJun stress kinase axis was upregulated in B6.Sst1S macrophages, as compared to B6, 12–36 hr of TNF stimulation, that is during the aberrant activation stage confirming persistent stress (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Moderate cell death was noted in B6.Sst1S macrophage cultures by 48 hr of TNF stimulation.
source: By 48 hr of TNF stimulation, we noted moderate cell death in B6.Sst1S macrophage cultures (Figure 3L, Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 3L and Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Treatments with Fer-1, BHA, or IFNAR1 blockade each prevented cell death in TNF-stimulated B6.Sst1S macrophages.
source: Treatments with Fer-1, the antioxidant butylated hydroxyanisole (BHA), or IFNAR1 blockade each prevented the cell death (Figure 3M), suggesting that both persistent stress and macrophage death were mediated by ROS, lipid peroxidation, and IFN-I pathway.
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: Persistent stress and macrophage death were mediated by ROS, lipid peroxidation, and IFN-I pathway.
source: Treatments with Fer-1, the antioxidant butylated hydroxyanisole (BHA), or IFNAR1 blockade each prevented the cell death (Figure 3M), suggesting that both persistent stress and macrophage death were mediated by ROS, lipid peroxidation, and IFN-I pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effects of inhibitors on cell death.

claim: IFNAR1 blockade did not restore Nrf2 and Ftl protein levels to wild type B6 levels at 8-12 hr of TNF stimulation.
source: The IFNAR1 blockade, however, did not restore the Nrf2 and Ftl protein levels, or the Fth, Ftl, and Gpx1 mRNA levels to the wild type B6 levels (Figure 4A-C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: LPO production was increased as early as 6 hr under TNF-stimulated condition in both B6 and B6.Sst1S prior to Ifnb1 superinduction.
source: Additionally, we observed that LPO production was increased as early as 6 hr under TNF-stimulated condition in both B6 and B6.Sst1S prior to Ifnb1 superinduction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by LPO assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Type I IFN signaling does not initiate LPO in the sst1 model.
source: These data suggest that type I IFN signaling does not initiate LPO in our model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of LPO production relative to Ifnb1 induction.

claim: IFNAR1 blockade did not prevent Ifnb1 mRNA superinduction.
source: Of note, the IFNAR1 blockade did not prevent the Ifnb1 mRNA superinduction (Figure 4D), thus rejecting a hypothesis that the Ifnb1 superinduction in B6.Sst1S macrophages was driven via an Ifnβ – IFNAR1 positive feedback (Ivashkiv and Donlin, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Ifnb1 superinduction in B6.Sst1S macrophages is not driven via an Ifnβ-IFNAR1 positive feedback.
source: Of note, the IFNAR1 blockade did not prevent the Ifnb1 mRNA superinduction (Figure 4D), thus rejecting a hypothesis that the Ifnb1 superinduction in B6.Sst1S macrophages was driven via an Ifnβ – IFNAR1 positive feedback (Ivashkiv and Donlin, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of effect of IFNAR1 blockade on Ifnb1 mRNA.

claim: IFNAR1 blockade suppressed Rsad2 mRNA expression, demonstrating efficiency of the blockade.
source: The mRNA expression of the interferon-inducible gene Rsad2, however, was suppressed, demonstrating the efficiency of the IFNAR1 blockade (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Treatment of B6.Sst1S macrophages with Fer-1 or DFO during initial TNF stimulation inhibited both Ifnb1 and Rsad2 mRNAs upregulation.
source: In contrast, treatment of B6.Sst1S macrophages with Fer-1 or the iron chelator DFO during initial TNF stimulation inhibited both the Ifnb1 and Rsad2 mRNAs upregulation (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C respectively).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Fer-1 treatment reduced Ifnb1 and Rsad2 levels in B6.Sst1S macrophages when added at 18 hr after TNF stimulation.
source: Importantly, Fer-1 treatment also reduced the Ifnb1 and Rsad2 levels in B6.Sst1S macrophages when added at 18 hr after TNF stimulation, that is during established aberrant response (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Lipid peroxidation is involved in both initial Ifnb1 superinduction and maintenance of IFN-I pathway hyperactivity during prolonged TNF stimulation.
source: Thus, lipid peroxidation was involved in both the initial Ifnb1 superinduction and in maintenance of the and IFN-I pathway hyperactivity driven by prolonged TNF stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effects of LPO inhibitors on Ifnb1 and Rsad2 expression.

claim: Blockade of IFNAR1 after 2, 12, or 24 hr after TNF stimulation prevented 4-HNE adducts accumulation at 48 hr.
source: Indeed, the blockade of type I IFN receptor (IFNAR1) after 2, 12, or 24 hr after TNF stimulation prevented the 4-HNE adducts accumulation at 48 hr (Figure 4H and I, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-G).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4H, I, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-G.

claim: Ifnb1 superinduction and IFN-I pathway hyperactivity in B6.Sst1S macrophages follow initial LPO production and maintain and amplify it during prolonged TNF stimulation.
source: Thus, Ifnb1 super-induction and IFN-I pathway hyperactivity in B6.Sst1S macrophages follow the initial LPO production and maintain and amplify it during prolonged TNF stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal relationship and effects of IFNAR1 blockade.

claim: No exogenous mouse viral RNAs were detected in B6 and B6.Sst1S macrophages before and after TNF stimulation.
source: No exogenous mouse viral RNAs were detected.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics analysis of transcriptomes.

claim: A select set of mouse LTR-containing ERVs and non-retroviral LINE L1 elements were expressed at basal level before and after TNF stimulation, but their levels in B6.Sst1S BMDMs were similar to or lower than those in B6.
source: A select set of mouse LTR-containing endogenous retroviruses (ERVs; Jayewickreme et al., 2021), and non-retroviral LINE L1 elements were expressed at a basal level before and after TNF stimulation, but their levels in the B6.Sst1S BMDMs were similar to or lower than those seen in B6 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: No evidence of transposon-derived dsRNAs was detected in macrophage small RNAs.
source: We also tested the accumulation of dsRNA using deep sequencing of macrophage small RNAs and failed to detect evidence of transposon-derived dsRNAs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Majority of basal transposon RNAs in macrophages exist primarily as single-stranded mRNAs that evade triggering interferon pathway.
source: We concluded from these findings that the majority of the basal transposon RNAs in macrophages exist primarily as single-stranded mRNAs that evade triggering interferon pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of dsRNA detection.

claim: Overexpression of persistent viral or transposon RNAs is excluded as a primary mechanism of IFN-I pathway hyperactivity in sst1-susceptible macrophages.
source: The above analyses allowed us to exclude the overexpression of persistent viral or transposon RNAs as a primary mechanism of the IFN-I pathway hyperactivity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the viral and transposon RNA analysis.

claim: IFN-I pathway hyperactivity in TNF-stimulated B6.Sst1S macrophages is driven by initial dysregulation of AOD and iron-mediated lipid peroxidation.
source: In contrast, they established that the hyperactivity of the IFN-I pathway in TNF-stimulated B6.Sst1S macrophages was itself driven by the initial dysregulation of AOD and iron-mediated lipid peroxidation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental findings.

claim: During prolonged TNF stimulation, IFN-I pathway acts as a potent amplifier of lipid peroxidation.
source: During prolonged TNF stimulation, however, the IFN-I pathway was upregulated, possibly via ROS/LPO-dependent JNK activation, and acted as a potent amplifier of lipid peroxidation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effects of IFNAR1 blockade and temporal relationships.

claim: Myc was regulated in an sst1-dependent manner: c-Myc mRNA was downregulated in TNF-stimulated B6 BMDMs but upregulated in susceptible macrophages.
source: First, we observed that Myc was regulated in an sst1-dependent manner: in TNF-stimulated B6 wild-type BMDMs, c-Myc mRNA was downregulated, while in the susceptible macrophages, c-Myc mRNA was upregulated (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: c-Myc protein levels were higher in B6.Sst1S cells in unstimulated BMDMs and 6-12 hr of TNF stimulation.
source: The c-Myc protein levels were also higher in the B6.Sst1S cells in unstimulated BMDMs and 6–12 hr of TNF stimulation (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Myc inhibitor 10058-F4 increased levels of Fth and Ftl proteins in TNF-stimulated susceptible macrophages.
source: Indeed, this treatment increased the levels of Fth and Ftl proteins in TNF-stimulated susceptible macrophages (Figure 5C)
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Myc inhibitor 10058-F4 decreased the labile iron pool in TNF-stimulated B6.Sst1S macrophages.
source: Indeed, this treatment increased the levels of Fth and Ftl proteins in TNF-stimulated susceptible macrophages (Figure 5C) and decreased the LIP (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by LIP assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Myc inhibitor 10058-F4 decreased levels of MDA, oxidized lipids, and 4-HNE adducts in TNF-stimulated B6.Sst1S macrophages.
source: Accordingly, the levels of MDA, oxidized lipid,s and 4-HNE adducts also significantly decreased (Figure 5E-G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: This is supported by assay data shown in Figure 5E-G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Myc inhibitor 10058-F4 decreased levels of Ifnb1, Rsad2, and ISR markers Trib3 and Chac1 in TNF-stimulated B6.Sst1S macrophages.
source: Accordingly, the levels of MDA, oxidized lipid,s and 4-HNE adducts also significantly decreased (Figure 5E-G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B), as well as the levels of Ifnb1, Rsad2, and the ISR markers Trib3 and Chac1 (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Myc promotes ribosome biogenesis, cap-dependent protein translation, and suppresses expression of ferritins in actively growing cells.
source: In actively growing cells, Myc promotes ribosome biogenesis, cap-dependent protein translation, and also suppresses expression of ferritins, most likely to provide labile iron for anabolic metabolism (Torti and Torti, 2002; Wu et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Torti and Torti, 2002; Wu et al., 1999).

claim: Myc hyperactivity is associated with cell senescence and maladaptive activity in the mTOR pathway.
source: Myc hyperactivity is associated with cell senescence and maladaptive activity in the mTOR pathway (Alic and Partridge, 2015; Hofmann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Alic and Partridge, 2015; Hofmann et al., 2015).

claim: In macrophages, Myc promotes development of myeloid-derived suppressor cells and alternatively activated macrophages.
source: In macrophages, Myc promotes the development of myeloid-derived suppressor cells and alternatively activated macrophages (Kumar et al., 2016; Pello et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Kumar et al., 2016; Pello et al., 2012).

claim: Myc hyperactivity is responsible for initiation of aberrant macrophage activation trajectory leading to increased labile iron pool and lipid peroxidation.
source: Here, we have shown that Myc hyperactivity was responsible for the initiation of the aberrant macrophage activation trajectory leading to increased intracellular labile iron pool (Fe+2) and lipid peroxidation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on Myc inhibitor experiments.

claim: Myc inhibition prevented Ifnb1 superinduction and activation of ISR markers Trb3 and Chac1.
source: Myc inhibition also prevented the Ifnb1 superinduction and activation of the integrated stress response markers Trb3 and Chac1.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: During prolonged TNF stimulation of B6.Sst1S macrophages, Myc hyperactivity and impairment of AOD lead to coordinated downregulation of ferritin chains and lipid peroxidation inhibitor genes.
source: During prolonged TNF stimulation of the B6.Sst1S macrophages, Myc hyperactivity and the impairment of AOD lead to a coordinated downregulation of the Ferritin heavy and light chains and lipid peroxidation inhibitor genes.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple experiments.

claim: Intracellular peroxidation of PUFA is catalyzed by ferrous iron via Fenton reaction and proceeds in autocatalytic manner.
source: In the absence of terminators, the intracellular peroxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) is catalyzed by ferrous iron (Fe+2) via the Fenton reaction and proceeds in an autocatalytic manner damaging cell membranes containing tightly packed PUFA (Mortensen et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mortensen et al., 2023.

claim: Autocatalytic lipid peroxidation fuels persistent oxidative stress and likely sustains JNK activity.
source: This autocatalytic lipid peroxidation fuels persistent oxidative stress and, likely, sustains the activity of JNK.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed persistent stress and JNK activation.

claim: Ifnb1 superinduction in B6.Sst1S macrophages leads to upregulation of interferon-inducible genes including PKR.
source: Downstream, Ifnb1 superinduction in B6.Sst1S macrophages leads to the upregulation of interferon-inducible genes, including PKR.
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited (Bhattacharya et al., 2021).

claim: PKR-dependent ISR activation leads to upregulation of Chac1, a glutathione degrading enzyme.
source: The subsequent PKR-dependent ISR activation leads to the upregulation of Chac1 (Bhattacharya et al., 2021) - a glutathione degrading enzyme gamma-glutamylcyclotransferase 1 (Crawford et al., 2015) that further compromises the AOD.
evidence: This is supported by citations (Bhattacharya et al., 2021; Crawford et al., 2015).

claim: Stepwise escalation locks susceptible macrophages in a state of unresolving stress maintained by continuous TNF stimulation and boosted by IFN-I signaling.
source: This stepwise escalation eventually locks the susceptible macrophages in a state of unresolving stress, which is maintained by continuous stimulation with TNF and boosted by IFN-I signaling.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings.

claim: During prolonged TNF stimulation of B6.Sst1S macrophages, autocatalytic lipid peroxidation and IFN-I hyperactivity form a positive feedback loop sustaining unresolving oxidative stress.
source: Thus, during prolonged stimulation of the B6.Sst1S macrophages with TNF, the autocatalytic lipid peroxidation and IFN-I hyperactivity form a positive feedback loop sustaining the unresolving oxidative stress.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings.

claim: The aberrant activation state did not immediately result in massive cell death but sustained a state that reduced macrophage ability to control Mtb.
source: Unlike ferroptosis, however, this did not immediately result in massive cell death but sustained a state of the aberrant macrophage activation that reduced their ability to control Mtb both in a cell-autonomous and a T-cell-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro infection data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In wild type B6 macrophages, Myc was inhibited more readily and ferritin proteins were upregulated to sequester free iron in parallel with upregulation of Nrf2.
source: In contrast, in the wild type B6 macrophages, Myc was inhibited more readily, and ferritin proteins were upregulated to sequester free iron in parallel with the upregulation of Nrf2.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2 and 5.

claim: Combined effects of Myc inhibition and ferritin upregulation increased stress resilience of activated B6 macrophages.
source: Their combined effects increased stress resilience of activated macrophages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences between B6 and B6.Sst1S macrophages.

claim: Ferritins and antioxidant pathways were upregulated in inflammatory macrophages isolated from Mtb-infected wild type B6 mice.
source: Recent in vivo studies also demonstrated that ferritins and antioxidant pathways were upregulated in inflammatory macrophages isolated from Mtb-infected wild type B6 mice (Pisu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pisu et al., 2020.

claim: Gradual accumulation of LPO product 4-HNE adducts was observed in BMDMs of both B6 and B6.Sst1S at 3-5 days post Mtb infection.
source: After macrophage infection with virulent Mtb in vitro, gradual accumulation of LPO product 4-HNE adducts was observed in BMDMs of both B6 and B6Sst1S genetic backgrounds at 3–5 days post infection (dpi).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: By day 5 post infection, TNF stimulation significantly increased LPO accumulation only in B6.Sst1S macrophages.
source: By day 5 post infection, TNF stimulation significantly increased LPO accumulation only in the B6.Sst1S macrophages (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Both Mtb-infected and bystander non-infected B6.Sst1S macrophages showed 4-HNE adduct accumulation.
source: Both Mtb-infected and bystander non-infected B6.Sst1S macrophages showed 4-HNE adduct accumulation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: TNF stimulation improved control of Mtb growth in B6 but not in B6.Sst1S macrophages.
source: TNF stimulation improved the control of Mtb growth in B6 but not in B6.Sst1S macrophages, as quantified using an Mtb replication reporter strain (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and D) and quantitative PCR of Mtb genomes (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy and qPCR data shown in Figure 6B, C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: LPO inhibition using Fer-1 improved survival of Mtb-infected BMDMs and prevented intracellular Mtb growth.
source: The LPO inhibition using Fer-1 improved the survival of the Mtb-infected BMDMs (Figure 6D-E) and prevented the intracellular Mtb growth (Figure 6F) during the five-day in vitro infection.
evidence: This is supported by cell survival and Mtb load data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: Iron chelator DFO significantly reduced Mtb growth in B6.Sst1S macrophages.
source: The iron chelator DFO also significantly reduced the Mtb growth, although restricting iron availability may also directly affect the bacterial replication.
evidence: This is supported by Mtb load data.

claim: Myc inhibitor F4 improved survival of Mtb-infected BMDMs and significantly reduced bacterial loads.
source: Importantly, the survival of Mtb-infected BMDMs was also improved, and the bacterial loads were significantly reduced by the Myc inhibitor, F4 (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: This is supported by cell survival and Mtb load data shown in Figure 6G and H.

claim: Effects of lipid peroxidation inhibitors became prominent between days 3 and 5 post infection.
source: Of note, the effects of the lipid peroxidation inhibitors became prominent between days 3 and 5 post infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that these inhibitors do not directly boost the bacterial killing by activated macrophages, but rather prevent macrophage damage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of inhibitor effects shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Immune T cells from BCG-vaccinated B6 mice significantly reduced Mtb loads in co-cultures with resistant B6 macrophages.
source: After co-culture with the immune T cells for 1 or 2 days, Mtb loads were significantly reduced in T cell co-cultures with the resistant B6 macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by Mtb load data shown in Figure 6J and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Susceptible B6.Sst1S BMDMs did not respond to immune T cells either in presence or absence of exogenous TNF.
source: The susceptible B6.Sst1S BMDMs did not respond to the same T cells either in the presence or absence of exogenous TNF (Figure 6I-J and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by Mtb load data shown in Figure 6I-J and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: B6.Sst1S BMDM responsiveness to T cells was improved by inhibitors of lipid peroxidation (Fer1) and Myc (F4).
source: The B6.Sst1S BMDM responsiveness to T cells was improved by inhibitors of lipid peroxidation (Fer1) and Myc (F4): the bacterial loads were significantly reduced 48 hr after co-culture with the immune T cells (Figure 6K, Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by Mtb load data shown in Figure 6K and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: T-cell-mediated Mtb control was specific for T cells isolated from BCG-immunized mice.
source: This T-cell-mediated Mtb control was specific for T cells isolated from BCG-immunized mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by control experiment data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1H.

claim: IFNAR1 blockade improved ability of TNF-stimulated B6.Sst1S macrophages to control Mtb with and without T help.
source: The IFNAR1 blockade improved the ability of TNF-stimulated B6.Sst1S macrophages to control Mtb with and without T help (Figure 6L, Figure 6—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by Mtb load data shown in Figure 6L and Figure 6—figure supplement 1I.

claim: IFNAR1 blockade restored responsiveness of TNF-stimulated B6.Sst1S macrophages to soluble IFN-γ.
source: It also restored their responsiveness to soluble IFN-γ that was inhibited by pre-stimulation with TNF (Figure 6M).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6M.

claim: During prolonged TNF stimulation of B6.Sst1S macrophages, Myc-driven lipid peroxidation and subsequent IFN-I hyperactivity compromise both cell autonomous and T-cell-mediated Mtb control.
source: These data demonstrate that during prolonged TNF stimulation of B6.Sst1S macrophages, the Myc-driven lipid peroxidation and subsequent IFN-I hyperactivity compromise both the cell autonomous and T-cell-mediated Mtb control.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple in vitro infection experiments.

claim: 4-HNE adduct levels dramatically increased in multibacillary lesions compared to paucibacillary lesions.
source: The 4-HNE adduct levels dramatically increased in multibacillary lesions (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Majority of 4-HNE+ cells in TB lesions were CD11b+ myeloid cells.
source: The majority of the 4-HNE + cells were CD11b + myeloid cells (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by fmIHC data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: 70 interferon type I and type II inducible genes were differentially regulated between Iba1+ macrophages in multi- vs paucibacillary lesions.
source: Among these, 70 genes were differentially regulated between the Iba1 + macrophages in multi- vs paucibacillary lesions (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by spatial transcriptomics data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Among upregulated genes in multibacillary lesions were Mmp12, IL6, Socs3, chemokines, p21, and many IFN-I target genes.
source: Among the upregulated genes were metalloprotease Mmp12, IL6, and Socs3, chemokines Cxcl10, Ccl2, Ccl3, Ccl4, Ccl19, cell stress and senescence marker p21 (Cdkn1a), and many known IFN-I target genes.
evidence: This is supported by spatial transcriptomics data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Most upregulated pathways in Iba1+ cells within multibacillary lesions were interferon, TNF, and IL6/STAT3 signaling.
source: The most upregulated pathways in Iba1 + cells within multibacillary lesions were interferon, TNF, and IL6/STAT3 signaling, and top transcription factors associated with upregulation of these pathways were NFKB1, STAT3, STAT1, and IRF1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 4D and E).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4D and E.

claim: Among IFN-inducible genes upregulated in paucibacillary lesions were Ifi44l and Ciita.
source: Among the IFN-inducible genes upregulated in paucibacillary lesions were Ifi44l, a recently described negative regulator of IFN-I that enhances control of Mtb in human macrophages (DeDiego et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2021) and Ciita, a regulator of MHC class II inducible by Ifnγ, but not IFN-I (Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is supported by spatial transcriptomics data in Supplementary file 8.

claim: Loss of local Mtb control in advanced pulmonary TB lesions was associated with accumulation of aberrantly activated macrophages containing lipid peroxidation products.
source: Thus, the loss of local Mtb control in advanced pulmonary TB lesions was associated with the accumulation of aberrantly activated macrophages that contained lipid peroxidation products, with upregulation of the IFN-I pathway and downregulation of Ifnγ-inducible genes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on spatial transcriptomics and immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Majority of YFP+ cells in TB lesions were Iba1+ macrophages, a fraction of which were iNOS positive.
source: The majority of the YFP + cells in TB lesions were Iba1 + macrophages a fraction of which were iNOS positive (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: This is supported by fmIHC data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 6A.

claim: Mice with paucibacillary lesions had 62% and multibacillary lesions had 80% activated macrophages expressing YFP.
source: The mice with paucibacillary lesions had 62% and multibacillary lesions had 80% activated macrophages expressing YFP.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of fmIHC data.

claim: Ifnβ is produced by activated M1-like macrophages in TB lesions.
source: These findings clearly demonstrated the production of Ifnβ by activated M1-like macrophages.
evidence: This is an inference based on co-localization of YFP and iNOS in macrophages.

claim: Stress markers phospho-cJun and Chac1 were primarily expressed by activated macrophages expressing iNOS and/or Ifnβ.
source: Next, we assessed the expression of stress markers phospho-cJun and Chac1 in total, IFN-I producing, and activated macrophages in TB lesions. These markers were primarily expressed by activated macrophages (Iba1+) expressing iNOS and/or Ifnβ (YFP+)(Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 6B-F).
evidence: This is supported by fmIHC data shown in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 6B-F.

claim: PKR was upregulated in multibacillary lesions, consistent with upregulation of upstream IFN-I and downstream ISR pathways.
source: We also documented the upregulation of PKR in the multibacillary lesions, which is consistent with the upregulation of the upstream IFN-I and downstream Integrated Stress Response (ISR) pathways, as described in our previous studies (Bhattacharya et al., 2021; Figure 7—figure supplement 7A).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 7A and citation to Bhattacharya et al., 2021.

claim: Progression from paucibacillary to multibacillary TB lesions is mechanistically linked with pathological macrophage activation characterized by escalating stress, Ifnβ upregulation, and IFN-I pathway hyperactivity.
source: Thus, progression from the Mtb-controlling paucibacillary to non-controlling multibacillary TB lesions in the lungs of TB-susceptible mice was mechanistically linked with a pathological state of macrophage activation characterized by escalating stress (as evidenced by the upregulation of phospho-cJun, PKR, and Chac1), the upregulation of Ifnβ and the IFN-I pathway hyperactivity, with a concurrent reduction of Ifnγ responses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on in vivo lesion analysis data.

claim: Stressed macrophages in TB lesions were unresponsive to T cell help.
source: In our in vitro experiments, these stressed macrophages were unresponsive to T cell help (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is an inference connecting in vitro and in vivo findings.

claim: Administration of BCG vaccine to Mtb-infected B6.Sst1S mice did not increase their survival.
source: Consequently, the administration of BCG vaccine to Mtb-infected B6.Sst1S mice did not increase their survival (Figure 7—figure supplement 7B).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 7B.

claim: Myc_up signature ranked within top 3 signatures with AUC of 0.74 and p-value of 0.008 in differentiating between TB treatment failures and controls.
source: Myc_up ranked within the top 3 signatures with an AUC of 0.74 and p-value of 0.008 (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of human blood transcriptome data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Myc_upregulated genes were enriched in TB treatment failure group relative to treatment control group.
source: Myc_upregulated genes were enriched in the treatment failure group relative to the treatment control group (Figure 8B, Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This is supported by ssGSEA analysis shown in Figure 8B and Supplementary file 9.

claim: Upregulation of Myc pathway in peripheral blood cells of TB patients is associated with poor prognosis and TB persistence.
source: These data indicate that the upregulation of Myc pathway in peripheral blood cells of TB patients was associated with poor prognosis and TB persistence even in patients infected with antibiotic-sensitive Mtb.
evidence: This is an inference based on the association of Myc signature with treatment failure.
